# Education in Finland: Summary
Finland’s education system emphasizes equity, child-centeredness, and lifelong learning. Early childhood education, considered foundational, is offered universally from eight months to six years, focusing on holistic development and social skills; formal schooling begins at age seven. Basic comprehensive education is compulsory and lasts nine years (grades 1–9), with recent legislation extending compulsory education to the age of 18 and including upper secondary school—either academic or vocational. Comprehensive schools are municipally run, have small class sizes, and operate without tuition fees—even in private schools—and advanced pupils are encouraged to support classmates. There are no "gifted" programs, and grading is non-standardized and typically follows a 4–10 scale. All students receive free school meals, materials, healthcare, and support services. Teachers are highly regarded, must hold a master's degree, and admission to teacher training programs is competitive.
Upper secondary education, now compulsory, offers academic or vocational tracks, both free of charge. Academic students complete the nationally graded matriculation exam, crucial for university entry, while vocational graduates can progress to polytechnics or university. Tertiary education comprises research-focused universities and industry-oriented universities of applied sciences; admissions are transparent, merit-based, and objective. Since 2017, tuition fees apply only to non-European international students. Finland’s adult education sector is robust, with opportunities for formal and non-formal learning, including open university courses and "Free Education" institutes for personal development. Finnish education abroad includes official Finnish-curriculum schools and “Finnish-inspired” models in other countries. National policies encourage proficiency in multiple languages and the integration of phenomenon-based learning alongside traditional subjects. The system is continually evolving, with reforms targeting efficiency and the global export of Finnish educational expertise.
